Chapter 8: The Internet’s Influence on Formal and Informal English
Have you ever sat down to write a cover letter, only to find your words feel awkward and stiff—especially after a whole day spent texting friends? Suddenly, every sentence seems too long. It’s almost like your brain is stuck in “internet mode,” and switching to formal writing just feels... weird.
You’re not alone. These days, the line between formal and informal English is blurrier than ever. Think about it: all those habits you pick up online—shortcuts, emojis, dropping punctuation—sometimes sneak their way into your emails or even your essays. And, let’s be honest, teachers and bosses are starting to notice. But here’s the thing—English has always had a fuzzy boundary between what’s “proper” and what’s “casual.” The internet just makes that fuzziness a lot more obvious.
Imagine a young professional, brand new to the working world, hesitating over how to end an email. Should they go with “Best,” “Thanks,” or maybe just their name? Meanwhile, in their group chats, nobody even bothers with a sign-off. The rules seem a bit random, but the pressure to get it right can feel huge.
Most of us end up learning how to code-switch, almost without thinking. In a work chat on Slack, a quick “got it” and a thumbs up emoji gets the message across. But when you’re writing to a client, suddenly, it’s all about full sentences and perfect punctuation. The internet hasn’t erased formality—it’s just given us more options to choose from.
Some folks worry that these online habits might be chipping away at our standards. But the truth? It’s a lot more nuanced. The internet actually makes us more aware of the choices we make with our words. We’re not losing the ability to write formally—we’re just getting better at switching between styles, depending on the moment.
And here’s something interesting: sometimes, the playful style of the internet even seeps into formal writing. You’ll see news headlines that borrow a bit of meme culture, or ads that toss in an emoji or some internet slang. The boundaries aren’t just blurry—they’re flexible, and ideas flow both ways.
So, is the internet replacing formal English? Not at all. If anything, it’s expanding our toolkit. Now, we’ve got more ways to be clear, more ways to be funny, and more ways to sound like ourselves. The real challenge isn’t about fighting these changes—it’s about understanding them, and learning when and how to use them wisely.
